title: Hainanese rice with Chaïneze, nice.
contentHtml:
Welcome back to Saturday (or Sunday depending on when we finish our Banh Mis) for another enlightening round of what we ate, why we ate it and how I happen to feel about it. Pay attention to the real details in this one. They could save your life.

(Also, sperm receptors in the brain??) … One thing at a time!

You’re in for a treat my fellow hungernauts, my hippocampal heroes, my cretans of culinary creations, my occipital observationalists, my sandwich psychopaths, my noodle nutcases, my monkeys of mozzarella.

Shut up!

Listen (read) closely.

If you live some place where this food is inaccessible or you’re completely unmotivated to trick your brain into doing it yourself, that’s fine too. Strap in for the ride and pray for mercy anyway. Kiss your past notions of chicken over rice good-bye.

Sayonara!

No more of this halal cart nonsense (though it is good, I’m not a monster). I’m yelling, screaming even, about Thai-Hainanese roast chicken over rice. Khao man gai (ข้าวมันไก่).

I’ll refrain from saying I was completely unaware that this existed, but I was, let’s say, unknowing. I’m most definitely late to the party on this one and I generally don’t like parties. This, however, my sweet sweet babies of broccoli, was some good ass chicken.

So how did this happen to little old me? I was browsing reddit (as you do) when I stumbled upon someone who was also in the midst of yelling about chicken. Intrigued, I see an image, similar to the one somewhere below, of a simple plate of nicely roasted chicken on rice. I see the price mentioned. $6.50.

What?

$6.50 for anything now is unthinkable, unimaginable and untenable I say! Unless it’s a plate of dumplings with watered down Sriracha. But, I believed my fellow chicken screamer and promptly started yelling at Cha to get ready to eat chicken for dinner. So we did as we normally do, strapped on our cool sun glasses, donned our New York approved outfits, and started smacking the side walk with our feet, clap-clap-clap, on the quest for $6.50 chicken over rice.

Along the two mile walk from Cha’s job to the chicken place, we “serendipitously” passed directly in front of our favorite Chinese skewer place on Grand street ‘Foodie BBQ & Bar’. Refer to last weeks article if you’re curious. We walked in, grabbed six lamb skewers, ate them in the doorway on the way out and continued on our way.

(Why someone hasn’t made a sandwich out of these guys is lost on me. Maybe that’s where we will make our millions Cha and I. Chinese skewer sandwiches).

After about forty-five minutes of parading our famished asses from 23rd street, through Union Square, past NYU, down the Bowery, across Delancey street and through the cramped chaos of Canal street, we found ourselves in clear view of the yellow awning that marked the beginning of our chicken fueled hedonic dream state where all recently formed frozen opinions of Manhattan’s Chinatown melted away and were washed down the drain.

Cha and I cracked open the door ready to take down as much chicken as we could handle. Hardly full off of three lamb skewers each, we were ravenous. Cha nearly ripped the handle off of the door as she walked in and I had to calm her down.

“We made it.” I assured her.

“I know.” She replied.

So there we were, in awe that we finally made it. And the screaming Redittor was right. $6.50, for a small at least, which in my eyes is good enough.

But we weren’t born scared and we are never ones to back down from too much chicken, so we went ahead spent the big bucks ($10.50) and got a large with ginger and garlic rice. When in Rome eat like the Romans you nincompoops. What was frankly exhilarating about Gai Kitchen was the choice to add a side of red curry to your plate of chicken for a few dollars extra. Sir, you have mistaken me for a coward. Yes we would like your curry. And add some drinks while you’re at it. Two Thai iced teas please, one for me and one for the lady. Tonight, we feast!

Shut up!

We mashed our order into the touch screen at the entrance , Cha tapped her phone on the sensor, transferring her hard earned money to Gai Kitchen where the fate of the night rested delicately in the hands of the cooks in the back. We said our prayers. We embraced tenderly understanding the risks we take are for the good of the world.

But we couldn’t take the suspense, and there were no seats for us, so we went outside to wait for our chicken. We walked down the street briefly and gazed at the crowd of tourists stuffing their faces with roast pork buns from Mei Lai Wah. Yum.

I couldn’t take it. I was nearly at my breaking point. The whole day was spent gripping my hair in confusion, anguish, pacing through work, images of chicken on rice flashing through my mind, and that number, $6.50, taunting me. Maybe I was scared. I forced Cha to return prematurely to Gai Kitchen where, upon entry, we managed to find a seat. Take that to-go we mentioned earlier, and keep it right here. We’re not going anywhere.

We sat down and suddenly, I hear the name called.

“Bob!”

The name I use at restaurants for takeout. Cashiers usually think I say “Paul” or “Tom” when I say “Colin”. I eat my words too. So I opted out of that name completely and went with “Bob” for simplicity. The best change I’ve ever made.

“That’s us” I said under my breath to Cha.

“I know.” She responded.

I launched out of my seat with a smile on my face, things moving in slow motion, and I made my way over to the counter.

“Bob?” He inquired.

“That’s me.” I replied smiling coyly . I took the bag of food out of his hands and turned around to see Cha grinning proudly, knowing I did it. We did it.

Once I made my way back to the table, I was like a nine year old who got a big lego set for Christmas and needed to immediately rip the package apart to get to the directions and start building as soon as possible.

“Okay, here’s the rice and chicken, there’s the curry, what’s that?”

“It’s soup.” Cha said. “They gave us chicken soup too. It’s a little spicy.”

Let me see. We dove into the chicken like the beasts we are. It was not disappointing.

For the price we paid the roast chicken was intensely juicy, nicely roasted and packed with that yes yes goodness. The rice filled with the ginger and garlic taste we were promised on the menu. And the curry on the side. How to win me over. Throw a side of curry anywhere and I’ll bend the knee. The Curry Slayer.

In no time, we finished the chicken and rice and were left with more curry which was quickly soaked up with another side order of rice.

“Bob!?”

Me again.

Down it went. We sat back (not too far though because no backs on those stools) and agreed simultaneously, that was pretty funkin’ good.

So we had done it. We successfully ate good chicken for a reasonable price and left happy as pigs in poop, knowing we would be back to satiate our chicken desires soon. Maybe not next week, or the week after, but soon.

SCIENCE BREAK:

Okay, now that the chicken is off my chest, we can really get down to business. I read a super interesting paper this week that was published in the journal Cell titled

Human-specific features of the cerebellum and ZP2-regulated synapse development1

What the absolute monk is that? I can hear you already. ZP2, or zona pellucida glycoprotein 2 is a receptor that is normally found on the egg of mammals. The zona pellucida, a protective barrier of the egg, is full of these glycoproteins and ZP2 is particularly important for sperm binding. That is all fine and dandy, birds and the bees, there’s a baby, cool, type of stuff.

What isn’t so wow-wow we know this already is that, in this study, when examining the cerebellums of four distinct primates (chimpanzees, marmosets, macaques and humans) ZP2 was found in the granule cells of humans which was distinct from the other three primates that were examined.

Imagine me, eating my chicken and circling back to this idea, rice falling from my mouth. There’s sperm receptors in human brains?

Shut up!

This is pretty cool! What does it mean? What does this actually do? Evolutionarily, why are our cerebellar granule cells full of these ZP2 guys and not the other primates? QUESTIONS!

This paper posits the idea that instead ZP2 is actually utilized as a sort of attenuator of synaptic growth in humans, allowing for a longer development period of the human brain, thus cooler stuff that we can do, different motor control! Though longer development (sad face) than other primates.

Obviously, or maybe not so obviously, that longer synaptic development period is crucial to us as humans. Yeah, we spend 15 years as dummies, ten as smarter dummies and the rest as slightly smarter, more tired dummies, but during those particularly dumb years, we are able to get in touch with some pretty not dumb things. Like Hainanese chicken or running multi-omic screens of primate cerebellums to see that there are actually sperm receptors in our brains. Questions answered, more questions unanswered. The cycle continues! So heres to the authors cited below who published this study and pour one out for the chicken who gave his life to fill our bellies on Friday night. He will be remembered fondly.

CML

Kim S, Cherskov A, Sindhwani A ...

Human-specific features of the cerebellum and ZP2-regulated synapse development

Cell, 2026; 189, 1802-1819.e28

title: Lamb skewers, beef sandwiches, we're really getting somewhere.
contentHtml:
It’s Saturday you little monks! Let’s get to the point. Friday night was as enlightening as it always is. A brisk walk through Chinatown in Manhattan to get our fix of Chinese red meat and cookies in rapid succession. No stomach ache, full of food and slightly smarter (we hope) than the day before.

QUICK DETOUR: Since starting research for the most recent anxiety x Colin collab, I’ve reached the next level of ‘wow’ realization on how the newest addition to our intellectual arsenal (Claude) could, should and will propel us into the future of research, medicine and understanding of our biology. People are noticeably scared of the ethical and environmental possibilities that this brings, but for me at least, I see this as an immensely powerful tool that we need to take advantage of and apply to better the rest of the world (don’t fuck it up). It will all come out in the wash (as they say!). I’ll spare the details of my personal adventures because this is presently a heavily trafficked area of writing, philosophizing, politicizing and polarizing where people who are much more qualified can speak much more eloquently to the topic. So, for now, my stance is most definitely in favor of the directions that our little computer wizards will take us in for the growth of science and humanity (up for change, debate, reflection and resurrection). DETOUR OVER

After finally getting some heat last week, we’re back down into the fifties and sixties with overcast skies and wind. What-ever, yo! Try and stop us! Last night, Cha and I got out of work, met at the apartment then immediately slapped the pavement with our sunglasses and cool outfits on. I had been thinking the entire day about going to get some spicy meat skewers in Chinatown. These little guys are usually found being slung from a cart throughout any of the Chinatowns in New York, but there is a small ‘hole-in-the-wall’ (cool) skewer place on Grand street that properly slings these bad boys, and offers a place to sit if you are so inclined. ‘Foodie BBQ & Bar’ or as the register says ‘Feng Shui Treasure Land’. If that name doesn’t make you want to get off your couch, smack your dad and then kiss him on the cheek then you have problems that only your personal religious guru can solve (God willing).

These tiny skewers (we get lamb) are pumped with sabor, strategically alternating between a chunk of meat, and a chunk of fat and doused in spicy goodness that leaves you screaming “Yeah!!!” at the sky with your arms outstretched, a true believer.

Shut up! I don’t believe you.

Well, no one asked you!

Go try them at a cart. It really doesn’t matter which one. All skewer carts are created equal and none of them disappoint (careful if next to the stinky tofu cart but that’s on you).

You can also choose from an assortment of other meats and vegetables for your skewer. You can even get a skewer with just corn kernels aligned nicely for the obsessive compulsives out there (I see you and understand).

So we sucked down a couple two-three lamb skewers, screamed at the sky a little bit more and proceeded to the next destination. We made our way around the corner and up one block to our very special ‘Spicy Village’ to tuck into some braised beef sesame pancake sandwiches.

My oh my, this sandwich. Take some beef, braise it, inject it with an exponential flavor function, slap two sesame pancake buns on the outside, cilantro in the middle, stop talking and be transported to a hallucinatory realm of flavor where you and Joe Rogan will finally sit down for that four hour conversation about vaccines and jiu jitsu. . .

Honestly though this sandwich might be one of the most consistently delicious, easy access things to get in the city that I have ever had. The pancake is crispy and the beef is salty, sweet, braised and shredded to almost a paste. Yabbba dabba doo.

So, Friday night was pretty nice. After eating the sandwich we ate a warm cookie on the side of the road and took donuts home from The Donut Pub at the 8th Street NYU station. C’est la putain de vie. Mais on est la maintenant watching the cat bite his blanket vigorously probably thinking about lamb skewers and their alternating meat then fat organization. I get it, homie.

In brain news, I learned the other day that celery seed contains l-3-n-butylphthalide (l3NBP), which turns out to be a pretty potent neuroprotective chemical1. This one little chemical guy here, L3NBP, effects dozens of different pathways not just in the brain but elsewhere in the body. So many different pathways even! G-protein coupled receptors, receptor tyrosine kinases and the AKT pathway are just one small piece of the pancake sandwich. In animal studies, it’s shown to reduce beta-amyloid (One of the Alzheimer’s bad guys implicated in cognitive impairment, to what extent still up in the air) induced cell death and is already used as an aid in protecting neurons after ischemic stroke2. Pretty muggy-buggin’ cool if you ask me! Now I’ll proceed to do no more research on the topic and eat a jar of celery seeds daily so I’ll never forget a single thing again. It has to be in someone’s stack right? Obligatory this is not medical advice.

Maybe a prophylactic against cognitive decline? Who knows. Read up on it! Though most of the studies on this compound are Chinese so it might do us some good to throw some muscle at it and see what we can get. The anti-oxidative and anti-inflammatory qualities are pretty cool though. Overall! Pretty cool findings, not sure how rigorous they are but still, the science is there and hopefully we can get some replications over here and move things alone. My grandfather had twelve siblings and all of his brothers fell ill with some kind of dementia either Alzheimers or dementia with Lewy bodies. Let’s get cracking on some more SCIENCE…please!

So until then Cha and I will eat our skewers on the sidewalk and take our donuts to go.

CML

Chen XQ, Qiu K, Liu H, He Q, Bai JH, Lu W. Application and prospects of butylphthalide for the treatment of neurologic diseases. Chin Med J (Engl). 2019 Jun 20;132(12):1467-1477. doi: 10.1097/CM9.0000000000000289. PMID: 31205106; PMCID: PMC6629339.

Huai Y, Dong Y, Xu J, Meng N, Song C, Li W, Lv P. L-3-n-butylphthalide protects against vascular dementia via activation of the Akt kinase pathway. Neural Regen Res. 2013 Jul 5;8(19):1733-42. doi: 10.3969/j.issn.1673-5374.2013.19.001. PMID: 25206470; PMCID: PMC4145956.

title: Beef Kala Bhuna
contentHtml:
I love eating so much food. I’m a skinny glutton who eats too fast! I love that we can taste anything in the first place. What type of beings are we anyway? Another time!

Evolution is pretty air tight at this point and we understand well enough why we, as mammals, would evolve preferences of non-rotten food, fresh meat and clean water to a carcass sitting in the sun being pecked at by raptors and tunneled through by maggots. The depths we plunge via our obsessive nature really brings out the most, not only in us, but in every aspect of the world we live in. Think about it! We went from eating raw meat off of dead animal bones to paying hundreds of dollars to sit down at a restaurant where a guy or gal has mastered their particular slice of the universe and has it prepared so your silly ass can eat it all up! Yummy yum yum.

So, get it while the getting is good! Eat all of the food while someone is good at cooking it you hungry little monkeys! Now is the time! We can TASTE god dammit! In a universe as excruciatingly large as this one is proving to be, how crazy is it to be a thing that tastes stuff and goes ‘mmm yes yes very good thank you thank you’ ? It’s certifiable. So certifiable in fact that I sit here and smash my keyboard about it while I could be outside prancing around Queens getting the spring sun into my eyes.

Tasters of things, connoisseurs of flavor with no training. It gets me thinking. Thinking a lot even! Thinking about the little tiny chemical guys that are in the food we eat, that make up the ingredients that make up the food we eat. The chemical friendships that form and break when we cook stuff and digest it in our bellies. How those little chemical guys make their way into our blood, swim around a bit with other little chemical guys, have a little chemical guy party and get shot up to our brain. Those little brain chemical guys do all sorts of things when they’re hanging out up there bumping around, saying hey to each other, swimming through synapses, passing through barriers. You wouldn’t even know!

So that’s the idea! When you’re eating your shepherds pie or whatever mum slapped on your plate, consider the path that food is taking from plate to tongue to brain and what that means for the fate of humanity.

That’s where my newest anxiety project is taking me. To the lands of flavor and chemical imbalances. Neuroses and noodles. Where cumin meets catecholamine. Where glutamate kisses Gran Marnier. You get the idea. Maybe better than me!

But we have to start somewhere. Out of all of the cool things to eat in the world, how do you choose just one to do your first brain x food collab deep dive? So I pulled from a hat located in the nether regions of my cognition for where to begin. I shuffled around a bit, moved some of the old furniture out of the way and dusted off the tiny walnut brain box I hid under a floor board way in the back there by the Santa dolls and old photos.

BEEF KALA BHUNA

Beef kala bhuna popped up. Of course it did! It all makes sense. What this dark, rich and spicy curry consists of could fill a neurochemistry text book. Just the mustard oil alone is controversial enough to get the FDA and the Lipid Association of India to battle it out over how dangerous or not dangerous this dish could be for us (stay tuned).

So that’s where we’re heading. Down a dark and spicy road. We might be tired, we might sweat from the top of our lips, we might even have to call out of work. It will all be worth it though. No mission is more important and no prize more desirous than to uncover the mysteries of beef kala bhuna. So stay tuned! Don’t touch that dial and prepare your belly with some pepto, lassi and a jug of water because you are in for the education you never asked for and never actually wanted! THANK YOU FOR YOUR ATTENTION TO THIS MATTER!

CML

title: Greek Easter
contentHtml:
We had no idea why the Greeks celebrate easter two weeks after the day my family usually asks if we would drive up to Massachusetts to spend the day with them for the holiest of days (we stayed in New York). As my grandfather said many years before I entered this world, ‘the church to which we belong is the ‘Church Of The Holy Mattress’, and Cha and I are steadfast in continuing this historical tradition. It turns out that it’s because Orthodox Christians like our beloved Greeks in Astoria use the Julian calendar for celebrating Easter instead of the Gregorian calendar. The more you know.

So we woke up today as we would on any other Sunday. At around 7:30 AM my eyes peel open and I quickly assault the bed in search of my phone to waste no time in catching myself up on the latest round of wisdom our dear leader has elegantly written and spread across the internet and into the minds of so many great Americans. God bless.

Cha had a late night on Friday and she is still recovering slightly so I leave her alone while I peruse the internet. I scroll past an array of interesting content: a lion who had lost a fight to an ambitious, younger alpha lion (alpha lion?), some guy broke into a person’s house, walked around a bit and I’m not sure what happened after that, legendary Indian singer Asha Bhosle passed away, known for her iconic and versatile voice, a handful of thinning haired men showed before and after images of them shaving it all off, and negotiations with Iran didn’t go so well. Let freedom ring!

Up and at ‘em. Coffee made, eat a banana and throw a handful of pills down my throat. The sun is out, the cat is fed and he wants to eat that mourning dove so bad.

Cha works very hard. Most days of the week she is at work from 8 am to 6 pm often tutoring afterwards and then studying for her anthropology degree after that. I frequently tell her, ‘take it easy at work and leave when your supposed to leave!’ and her reply is always ‘but we need the money’. Can’t argue with that logic.

Since it’s Sunday, we go to get our weeks supply of fruit from United Brothers Fruit Market or as we call them ‘The Fruit Guys’. Big bag of apples, big bag of pears and a bushel of bananas baby, NOW WE’RE COOKING! We need some bread in our bellies though so we instantly make the assumption that we can pop into the Greek supermarket ‘Mediterranean Foods’ off of 30th ave to grab two spinach pies for $3. We turn the corner and I remember out loud,

‘Greek Easter, they’re closed.’

Across the street a restaurant has a lamb spinning over hot coals with smoke billowing into the street. No time for a full brunch though and honestly, fuck brunch! Maybe we get a burek? The delicate spiral balkan meat pie always fills the stomach and resets anything that the nights sleep rejuvenated. Nah. Keep it light and stick to the fruit. I drop Cha off at a cafe a few miles from home that has a quaint back yard conducive to focus, relaxation and caffeination. I take off to grab coffee for the week and pick up my road bike from the shop for its yearly tune-up. I am still quite famished.

While walking back to the house I’m left with the question pulsing in my brain, ‘what can I eat?’ Luckily I decided to take 31st ave back to the house which lays me up directly into the arms of one of the most dedicated food-trucks to exist. Franky’s Souvlaki.

Franky’s Souvlaki was started by yes, Franky, in 1970. What was a small hot dog style cart fifty something years ago is now a fleet of full-sized food trucks dishing out souvlaki sticks, sandwiches, rice platters and other good stuff every day of the week. Franky’s on 31st ave is a mainstay of our corner of Astoria. You can always pop up and grab something quick to satiate yourself no matter the weather, holiday or political climate.

Franky’s Greek Souvlaki truck being open on Greek Easter Sunday was my biblical miracle, my oasis in the desert, my prayer answered. My Christ even! Blasphemers rejoice! My hunger was eradicated within forty seconds by the quickest transaction that can be made on the street (I think). I got my Souvlaki drenched in sauce and fresh off the grill and it took me all of two minutes to erase it from existence.

It dawned on me at that moment, my consistent patronage of this institution on 31st ave is my Sunday worship. My offering to God, my acceptance of the imperfection of man and the sins I wish to wash away! Franky’s was there when I needed guidance and it gave me the sustenance I needed to carry on through the day.

One lamb with everything as I always get. Leave a dollar as my offering in the basket. Peace be with you, Franky.

I am the furthest from a religious person. Most of the stuff said in the Bible or Qu’ran and the ‘lessons’ taught come across as dated doctrine that have no utility in modern society. On Greek Easter though, I abandon my worship of thine Holy Mattress and assume my position as a follower of the true savior of man, the lamb of God, Franky’s Souvlaki.

One lamb with everything, I’ll have it for now.

p.s. We went to Flushing later on in the day and got more Chinese lamb skewers with some spicy powder on them. Very good yes yes very good.

CML

title: Fried Whiting
contentHtml:
Applying to grad school has been as expected. Stress-laden, hunger-generating, self doubt-exacerbating fun times. It’s my first time applying to grad school and I never realized the amount of self you need sell to an admissions committee. How do you tell someone that you’ve never met that you’re ‘definitely’ qualified to be admitted but not come off as a know-it-all though you obviously know next to nothing? I’m not sure. I did my best. I do think I am a good candidate for the program I applied to but I also recognize the blaring deficits in my application. I’m a hobbyist at best with brain related things. Maybe that’s enough this time around?

There’s an amorphous pit in the depths of my mental space that never seems to be filled. I’ll do this today! I’ll do this today! I’ll do this today! Make a painting, write a paragraph, model a hook for Cha’s towel, 3D print it, read a paper, walk around the block, do a kick-flip, ruminate, ruminate, ruminate, change our future plans, change them again, let’s move out of New York, never-mind we’ll live here forever!! It is insane. It’s normal for most people, right?

So one step at a time. I’ll apply to grad school. I can’t be distracted if I’m in school at least. Like that I’ll know I’m actually getting something finished instead of thinking about it endlessly until I inevitably change my mind and attack another hobby like a rabid dog until it seems lifeless. Then I’ll walk away waiting for a stroke of inspiration to smack me in the face and get me moving again. Inspiration or anxiety?

We did eat some good fish this past weekend. Taverna Kos, a sanctuary place for us in New York. It’s a small Greek restaurant in Astoria that for the longest time I thought was some sort of social club where only 70 year-old pappous were allowed. A few years ago I walked past it on one of my ‘walk around the block moments’ saw a group of non-70-year-old-pappous inside and texted Cha notifying her that I had found a place we must try. How cool are we? Childless 30 year olds with a little extra cash (not much honestly) living in New York City. Why aren’t we influencers anyway? Send US your money! RESTAURANT RECOMMENDATIONS PEOPLE for when you plan your next trip to the big apple, the center of the world, your dream vacation!

We spend our money on food and that pretty much sums it up. Well other things too like cat food and gas for the car and wine during the winter, beer in the summer. Anyway, since we had both been pretty stressed about normal things like work, school and war, the arrival of a break in the darkness of this year’s frigid winter started us prancing our way to Taverna Kos for our first meal of the year there.

‘What are we going to get?’ The usual question as we walk the 20 minutes from home. It’s a pretty simple answer when we go to Kos because the way we do it we get filled up with good fish, a few pints of Greek beer and lemon potatoes all for about 40 bucks. So that’s what we did of course! Fried whiting that has a different size portion every time, a spicy feta cheese dip with grilled pita called tirokafteri and a side of lemon potatoes. The lemon potatoes man. What are they doing to those? Do they get marinated in lemon juice? I’m too scared to ask. They cut like butter but have a bit of a chewy skin from being roasted under the salamander. Very good, yes yes, very good.

We get caught up in our stuff Cha and I.

When we first got to the restaurant this time around we weren’t met with the same tranquility that we were used to. In fact it was the opposite. There were two huge parties of boisterous people in the tiny restaurant that were celebrating something together. The restaurant is a right angle around the corner of a block that fits 6 tables around its perimeter. The two parties hugged the corner and we were sandwiched between. At other restaurants the noise would drive me insane, and it should have in this instance if I’m being honest. But, I knew that Taverna Kos is for this exact purpose. These two loud ass families were getting after it together, in the exact place they should be getting after it. It made more sense when we understood that the owner of Taverna Kos, a younger guy, was the host of the party. He apologized to us even though we didn’t need any apology (the potatoes solve many problems) and he brought us two more rounds of beer.

A lesson: everything is pretty much okay even if it’s loud, and if you wait it out patiently, you’ll get a beer.

CML

p.s.

title: Shrimp
contentHtml:
There are a variety of ways to prepare crustaceans just as there is a multitude of crustaceans to be prepared. Boiled with peppercorn and lemon, sautéed with butter and garlic, grilled, deep fried, dehydrated, or eaten totally raw, these armored sea creatures harbor a flavor that induces a hypnotic pleasure state that can rip you out of this backwards reality we live in and transport you to a nirvana of salt and acid. What’s happening when we eat crustaceans that allows us to probe the hedonic centers of our brain, getting our salivary glands to work on overdrive? It’s complex to say the least and can be examined through a behavioral, neurobiological, gustatory and cultural lens. First however, gotta get some shrimp.

AbuQir, a tiny seafood restaurant on Steinway street in Queens, provides some of the most consistently delicious, no-frills Egyptian style seafood that is accessible in the tristate area. Like most seafood restaurants in this vein, you walk in and assess the landscape of ice trays filled with fish laid out in front of you. Scallops, tiger shrimp, bronzino, octopus, striped bass, calamari, sardines, and all of the other staples at your disposal. You’re free to choose what protein suits you best, but that’s where your choices end.

Restaurants like AbuQir limit the ways that the seafood can be prepared on purpose to avoid any challenges associated with providing a plethora of different styles of cooking. They want their product to be consistent and predictably stimulating for every customer, so they trim the confounding variables and blast off with their tried and true techniques. There is no time for fooling around. When we order these shrimp, we don’t even specify how we want them cooked, we just tell them how many we want and they always come out as they are pictured above. We are never disappointed.

So why are crustaceans so good?

The Shell

The shell of the crustacean is the hook on which everything else hangs when it comes to enjoying these little guys. Think about it. Why do we enjoy pistachios in the shell or ballpark peanuts so much? We have to work for them. If you ever buy shelled pistachios that you can throw in to your mouth, dozens at a time, they don’t produce the same gratifying pleasure response as the ones in the shell. We need to work for each little bit of pistachio we get from them, and this limits us to eating one at a time.

What keeps us from going mad during a pistachio binge is that the work is not too demanding. If we had to use a vice and a hammer each time we wanted to eat a pistachio, we would reconsider and go for the potato chips even though the pistachio is better tasting. However, with proper technique, you can crack through the shell of a pistachio with relative ease. The same goes for shrimp. When they’re cooked and served in their shells you can’t inhale a plate of shrimp like you would inhale a bag of potato chips. Instead, you need to work a little to enjoy every bit of each shrimp.

This effort directly involves the pleasure and reward processing center of our brains. More precisely, the nucleus accumbens. This is the all too famous or infamous area of the brain that is implicated in pleasure, reward seeking and addiction. Without getting bogged down with jargon, essentially, the nucleus accumbens releases dopamine (a monoamine neurotransmitter) in response to pleasurable experiences which generates a motivation to continue the behavior. You eat one shrimp, integrate the flavor you’re working with, sacrifice a little bit of time to work for the next one by releasing it from its shell prison, and continue the cycle of pleasure seeking until the plate is cleared and your stomach is full.

Behavior aside, the shell also holds flavor. Anyone who has taken a cooking class or watched any show on The Food Network understands that the bones, shells, heads and all of the other funky parts of an animal are filled with flavor. It’s the reason we save the fish heads to make a fish stock, or hold onto the beef bones for roasting to make a demi-glace. There’s flavor in there! So not only does the shell convince you that it’s worth it to eat more shrimp, it’s enhancing the experience of pleasure by providing more flavor than if the shrimp had been cooked naked.

Finger Food

Most crustaceans that we eat are inherently a finger food. Crabs, and lobster have to be meticulously broken down with our hands to preserve every morsel of protein that exists under the tough exterior. Shrimp, although they can be eaten with a fork or chopsticks, almost seem like they were designed as a savory animal lollipop. The tail placed perfectly to grab on to, to swirl the body in some butter with garlic and throw it in your mouth to strategically use the pressure created by your fingers and teeth to ensure that you get all of the meat out from the inside of the tail.

Finger foods like this generate a deeper intimacy with our meal by increasing the direct food to body stimulus we receive while eating. You become one with the shrimp as your fingers become coated in minced garlic, olive oil and shrimp pieces. The sensation only diminishes after you’ve eaten the shrimp and promptly cleaned your fingers of leftovers with your lips and tongue just to be tidied up with a napkin that never holds up to the job.

The nerves in your fingers send signals to your brain at the same time the chemical messages relayed to your tongue are being shuttled up. It’s an incredible circuit. The chemical and mechanical sensations related to your mouth are sent from the source to the brain via nerves. Taste sensations via facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) and mechanical/textural sensations via trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V). You can read more about this here. These chemical and mechanical signals shoot up from your mouth to your brain in just under a second and lay everything into your conscious mind for your enjoyment.

There is a lot more happening behind the scenes, like the use of other nerves and various brain regions working in tandem to integrate all of the sensations involved in tasting, eating, handling and enjoying your shrimp. This is why it is impossible to lump any one experience into one single pathway and if it weren’t the case, we would forget the flavors associated with our favorite food. Imagine tasting shrimp for the first time every time you ate shrimp!

Lean

Shrimp, like other crustaceans, are incredibly lean animals. One shrimp tends to have less than 0.5 grams of fat with the remaining majority being good protein. In fact, when comparing 85 grams of shrimp to the same quantity of other shellfish, the shrimp came in with the least grams of fat at 0.45 grams. This lack of naturally occurring fat allows for preparations of shrimp and other crustaceans to range massively. When we think of shrimp, we can imagine them fried, boiled, grilled, steamed, ground into paste, sautéed, whatever you want and this is partly due to the lack of fat present in the shrimp. Its one reason we don’t do battered and deep fried salmon. Salmon already has a high fat content which limits the way it should be cooked. Shrimp on the other hand welcomes additional fat to coat the protein and smooth out the acid from the lemon wedge that we add on top.

The leanness of shrimp is a reason that they tend to be recognized as a very healthy protein to ingest. Although shrimp are lean, the small fat content in them is generally made up of omega-3 fatty acids which have health benefits for the heart and brain-especially since the brain is comprised of 50-60% lipids with about 35% being omega-3 fatty acids. These lipids make up the white matter in the nervous system which is critical in maintaining proper neuronal signaling and protection of the axons of neurons.

SO!

Clearly shrimp are a powerful species that we enjoy for many reasons. We can snack on them, we can dine on them, we can savor every morsel or we can mix them in with pasta or throw them on top of rice. Alongside their crustacean cousins they provide us with a flavor that seems like we should feel guilty about it. Though, when cooked correctly, they can provide us with vital nutrients that support proper functioning of our bodies. With proper functioning bodies, we can stick around a while longer to enjoy the things that life has to offer. Love, sunlight, air, the existential angst that goes alongside being a human being, or the joy that counters it. Thank you shrimp, and thank you AbuQir. I will be seeing you soon.

CML

title: Tacos
contentHtml:
Cha and I went to Orlando a few weeks ago because we had been wanting to go to Universal Studios for some time. Since before we got married we had been reminiscing on when we had gone to amusement parks like Universal as kids and how fun it seemed and how excited we were to do it again as adults. When we arrived in Orlando, the magic was vacuumed out of the atmosphere when we realized that the once enchanted place that we remembered as kids was actually a wasteland of highways gift shops and T.GI. Friday’s.

Not a problem, we still had the park to get to in the morning and that held hope for us. We got to the park nice and early and quickly got onto a roller coaster, which up until then was my favorite thing to do at amusement parks. I always loved roller coasters, but I realized that my neck muscles weren’t what they used to be and the headache that followed stayed put for the remainder of the day only to be dulled by some emergency acetaminophen that I packed.

Two bummers, but okay. We made it through and Cha got to see what she really wanted to see which was the Harry Potter universe nestled in the back of the park. This is a pretty amazing situation they have going on and was the proper rebound we needed to keep our heads high.

All was more or less going to plan until we reached The Hulk. The infamous Hulk. I’m not sure why but I have a tendency to assume that I always have the correct method for everything even though this has been proven wrong on enough occasions that it pains me to even write this. Now I knew that my glasses would be an issue on roller coasters, but I didn’t want to miss anything going on in the line so I kept them on instead of storing them in the lockers that are provided at each ride for FREE. Cha offered to keep my glasses for me but I insisted that ‘no they’ll be fine with me’. “No worries!” I thought. I’ll put them in my pocket (my notoriously loose pocket) of my nike running pants while riding and everything will be fine. Moron.

The Hulk ride shoots you at a 30 degree angle through a tube and it pulls one g of force. It performs the normal loops and hard turns that any roller coaster would and ensures that all neck muscles are sufficiently stressed before returning to the surface of Earth. We pull in after the ride, my head killing me and I touch my pocket, no glasses. I know the reaction I’ll get from Cha, because I’ve done this so many times. In fact, a similar thing happened in Mexico when I decided to jump into a cenote with my glasses on where they promptly exited the comfort of my face and sank to the bottom of a God knows how deep hole in the Earth filled with water. The feeling of embarrassment is like no other and the shame that reels in your body from your toes to the top of your head is like you’ve been emptied of all vitality and it has been replaced with a shivering anxiety ridden pond muck that sticks to all surfaces of your interior. Oh, and you can’t see anymore.

The thing is, it actually wasn’t too bad once I lost the glasses. I brought an extra pair so I wouldn’t be without them indefinitely had something happened. However, we didn’t want to leave the park to wait in line again to enter so I persevered the rest of the day with low visibility.

We enjoyed the day as we normally do, and when it was time to leave, the feeling of getting my eye sight back was filling me with a type of joy that only those who can’t see well understand. We were walking out of the front gates when Cha mentioned that she wanted to bum a cigarette off of someone and she promptly found a nice enough looking guy who was smoking by himself outside of the park.

“Go over there because there is a better chance he gives me a cigarette if you’re not around” She told me.

I walked away and waited, only to be called back awkwardly when she mentioned to him that she was here with her husband (me) and I was for some reason lurking in the distance pretending to be on my phone searching for my lost wife.

I met the guy, we’ll call him Brian, and he was a 50 year old, chain smoking, long black hair having, eighteen year old girl dating, Florida son of a bitch. He was nice enough though and he mentioned that he had season tickets to Universal and he regularly travels there from Jacksonville with his son, who was at the outdoor bar sending himself closer and closer to a black out as the minutes passed.

I smelled the eau de Trump a mile away, and as it wafted over me in golden waves my MAGA detectors started sounding. I’ll put that to the side for a free cigarette outside of Universal Studios though. Once we finished our cigarettes and brief conversation, I mentioned that we had to go get my extra glasses from the car as our escape plan, but my lovely wife Cha, whom I adore beyond possibility, is French and is culturally blind to the dichotomy that exists in the United States currently. She recommends that we stay and hang out with him and his son some more as a way to say thanks for the smokes. I get it, and maybe I’m the ass, but I was fine with taking the cigarette and getting out of there.

Anyway, we return to formally meet the son, who is about thirty years old. He had made an inverse effort to introduce himself to us which was an interesting show of his manliness at the outdoor bar at Universal Studios. He slowly but surely, like so many conservatively minded nowadays do, started asserting his political dominance over us completely unprovoked. He made it apparent that he detested everything about the northeast of the United States (without spending any time there) and proceeded to lecture about how Boston is a shit hole city and France is just about the same.

We take the blows, our homelands were under attack but we stood strong. That was until he said one thing that threw me for a loop. We mentioned the Mexican food and general latin cuisine that he was missing out on by being so opposed to anything about New York City and he quickly responded, disgusted,

“No, no, fuck Mexican food. Taco Bell maybe but Mexican food is garbage.” He said this in a way that seemed more directed towards Mexican people than cochinita pibil.

To each his own, but for me, that was the line.

“That is the wildest thing I’ve ever heard, you don’t like tacos?” I jabbed back.

Only for him to disregard us completely and in a moments notice, up and vanish without paying with his equally drunk father to drive two hours home at 8:30 at night from Universal Studios in Orlando, Florida on a beautiful night in March 2025. Into the night they went, our two heroes defending our great nation from the treachery of Mexican food.

This circumstance was interesting to say the least. We were accused of being in on their scam until we returned to clear our name with the bartender. It did reinforce my love for tacos though. Last Friday we went back to our favorite Taco place in Astoria, Los Nuevo Portales, which still has individual tacos for under $4. Two suadero and two chorizo for me and two al pastor and two suadero for Cha. La vie est belle or viva los tacos or something like that.

The moral of the story is, never let someone talk shit about one of your favorite foods without pressing them on it until they vanish unexpectedly into a Floridian night with their drunken father with whom they were spending the day with outside of Universal Studios fighting the woke mob that is oppressing us day in and day out.

God bless America.

CML

title: Can Your Favorite Restaurant Do No Wrong?
contentHtml:
When you make a return trip to your favorite restaurant, your expectations that the experience will be pleasant outweigh the concerns that something catastrophic will take place. You use this confidence to get past the doubt that your preferred cut of beef could turn its back on you, sending you to the ER for an IV to replenish those electrolytes lost to the universe. I’ll call this the “do no wrong” restaurant bias. This bias is one that many of us hold in some way whether we believe it or not.

Why is your favorite restaurant your favorite restaurant? Would it still be your favorite if this restaurant were to suddenly disobey the standards you set and send you to the hospital? How do these expectations live in your cognitive landscape to create a vibrant existence that does not require a fine-tooth comb, a pair of tweezers and a scanning electron microscope to understand the intricacies of everyday experiences? Let’s start with some food.

Queens in New York is a mecca of world of cuisines that are otherwise completely out of reach for the rest of the United States. For those in less densely populated areas of America, tasting Nepalese momo or Bangladeshi biryani is something that could potentially never happen, but for residents of Queens, these, and hundreds more dishes can be tasted any day of the week. For most of us here, we frequent a handful of places that embody the “do no wrong” bias of restaurants and allow us to venture into a culinary demimonde that can be intimidating, off putting or potentially hazardous to our health.

In this case, the ‘do no wrong’ bias means that, regardless of obvious signs of health-code violation, uncomfortable seating arrangements, indifferent wait staff or an air duct bolt in the ravioli, we continue to dine at and prefer the food of this restaurant over others in the immediate vicinity with similar offerings.

I should clarify that I am not saying that this is a hard and fast rule that people prefer to eat at restaurants that create a sense of risk to dine at. What I am getting at is that there are places in which, against our normal judgment, we allow ourselves to venture past dining norms and risk a little bit to get a taste of what we normally would not.

This bias can come from many different places. One of the more common in NYC is the voucher made by trusted friends, family, comrades, coworkers, doormen, baristas, neighbors and so on. Emphasis on trusted here. This voucher is the first method of barrier deconstruction that pushes us past any preconceived opinions that we may have had, had we stumbled upon the restaurant on our own while walking down the street.

Since our brains are pattern seeking organs that do their best to recognize regularly occurring patterns with clarity, it’s obvious why the advice of a trusted friend or family member would be enough to send us in to a restaurant we would not normally venture to. The pattern of advice that was given to us from this person must have relatively consistent positive returns - or else they wouldn’t be our friend - thus the recommendation to try this new ‘riskier’ restaurant comes with little hesitation. Our friend’s recommendation paints a picture of the restaurant before we even arrive and taste any of the food. It primes us to like what we’re eating, understand the cultural variability and try the spicier squid. This newly painted mental representation of the restaurant fills in any of the cognitive gaps that you might trip over had you not been given a context to the restaurant as a whole.

“Why do they eat everything with their hands?” “Will I fall through that hole in the booth?” “Is that steam table on?” Concerns bombard you and you break a sweat, but your trusted friend has given you the key that unlocks the first, iron clad door. The recommendation that pushes you past your hesitation.

My wife Cha and I started going to a Colombian/Ecuadorian restaurant in our neighborhood a couple of months ago under the recommendation of my Uncle who lives down the block. He is known for solid recommendations for food, and I trust his judgment wholeheartedly. When he first mentioned the restaurant to us, it was because we were searching for a roasted chicken place that wasn’t going to cost us seventy something dollars, like some unnamed Manhattan establishments are capable of getting from you. He recommended we try ‘Sandro’s Latin Food Restaurant’ on 23rd ave in Queens. His text was cryptic,

‘Combo #1 Whole Chicken

Rice beans

Salad

,21.00

Not bad’

Perfect. Even though it took us a few months to finally make it over to Sandro’s, it was worth the wait. This was originally where I had the realization that the smallest nudge by a recommendation is the prejudice crushing tool necessary for the expansion of culinary adventures. We walked in and enjoyed a half roasted chicken, “La bandera de pollo Sandros” they called it (not the original recommended whole chicken) with a criminally large plantain, rice, beans, avocado and two empanadas for under twenty dollars. How could this be? We are spoiled in New York.

.

While we were eating, I looked out the front window and noticed something I had not when walking in. Sandro’s Latin Food Restaurant had a B. Now this really is not a deal breaker. People generally know the level of scrutiny that the department of health puts restaurants through for their health inspection. A spoon in the sauce? Points! Line cook with the health certification walking in as the inspection is wrapping up? Points! You get the idea. It has tendency to be petty and unfair but does serve a purpose which I think people appreciate by avoiding campylobacter jejuni most times they go out.

Anyway, Sandro’s had a B. Honestly, for a place like Sandros, it is unassuming enough on the outside that I would have walked by, possibly considered it, seen the B then continued on my way. However, the recommendation made to me by my uncle pushed me through the barrier that I had not even realized was there.

We were in and eating! It was too late to change our minds, the chicken was outrageous and the rice and beans madonne! It was one of those places where Cha and I look at eachother with full mouths and say “…so fucking good…” before looking back down to keep eating in silence. Put Sandros on the list wesh.

So we made it and Sandros had parked itself in a corner of my mind that will allow me to overlook its imperfections indefinitely. What I wonder though is if we had walked in on our own without a recommendation, how would our experience have been? Would we have been so accommodating to the B grade? Would that have tainted my taste buds and pushed us away from finding the joy in the chicken? The beans even?

We’re funny, manipulable creatures. Just tell us something and we believe it to be true. Maybe I’m just easily manipulated. But what form of evolutionary process made us so prone to placebos and why are they so cool for us? I’ll think about it over some chicken.

To be continued…

CML
